lesson_title: One Cheque, Two Sources: Companies and Their Unique Transactions
hook_text: The company wrote one cheque for R360 000 to buy back its own shares — but the books split it into R230 000 and R130 000. Here's why.
clip_script: Naledi's spaza started with airtime, bread and paraffin. Now it's a building-supplies yard, and contractors want her in three more towns — but the bank has lent what it will lend. So she registers a company and sells SLICES of it. Buy a slice and you own a piece of the yard, a claim on its profits, without stacking a single bag of cement — and the most you can ever lose is what you paid. That promise is limited liability. Now the entry that catches everyone. Over the years the company sold 800 000 slices for R4 600 000 — an average of five rand seventy-five each. Then a founding shareholder retires, and the company buys his 40 000 slices back at nine rand each: R360 000. But the capital account never received nine rand for those slices — on average it received five seventy-five. So capital returns exactly what it held, R230 000, and the other R130 000 comes out of saved-up profits: retained income. One cheque, two sources — a refund of capital plus a farewell share of old profits. And the returned slices? Shredded. The yard is now cut into 760 000 slices, so every remaining slice just got bigger.
visual_style: A corner spaza morphing into a timber-and-cement yard; slices of a loaf handed over a counter for rand notes; at the buy-back, a single cheque tearing into two labelled halves — capital refund and profit farewell — before the returned slices are shredded.
pacing: Fast story open, deliberate slow-down on the one-cheque-two-sources split, sharp close on the shredded slices.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and handle any share issue, buy-back, tax or dividend question with one rule each.
